summary: Defines version 2 of the Generic Security Service API, which gives programs security services in a generic way across different underlying mechanisms. It was replaced by RFC 2743.

eli5.summary: It is a common plug that lets programs use many security tools without rewriting.

questions: how does gss-api establish a security context
subtitle: A generic programming interface that lets applications get authentication and message protection without caring which security technology sits underneath.

tldr.problem: Protocols and applications need strong authentication, integrity and confidentiality, but each security technology (Kerberos, public-key systems and others) has its own interface, which ties applications to one of them.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API defines mechanism-independent calls for acquiring credentials, establishing a security context between peers by exchanging opaque tokens, and then protecting individual messages with calls such as GSS_Wrap and GSS_GetMIC.
tldr.outcome: Applications gain source-level portability across mechanisms. Version 2 revises RFC 1508 incrementally and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2743.

today: RFC 2078 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 1508 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2743, so the current GSS-API version 2 specification is there.

sections.title: What GSS-API Does
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service API (GSS-API) gives callers security services in a generic way, supportable with a range of underlying mechanisms and technologies, which allows source-level portability of applications. A typical caller is itself a communications protocol that wants to protect its traffic with authentication, integrity and/or confidentiality.

The RFC defines services and primitives independent of both mechanism and programming language. It expects two companion kinds of document: language bindings (such as the C bindings of RFC 1509 for version 1), and per-mechanism documents defining token formats, protocols and procedures. This memo revises RFC 1508 with specific, incremental changes made in response to implementation experience and liaison requests.

The stated design goals are mechanism independence (secret-key technologies such as Kerberos or public-key approaches such as X.509), protocol environment independence, protocol association independence, and suitability to a range of implementation placements, both inside and outside a trusted computing base.
sections.eli5: Different locks need different keys. GSS-API is one standard key slot, so your program can use any lock without being rebuilt.

sections.title: Credentials, Tokens, Contexts, Mechanisms and Names
sections.content:
Credentials are the prerequisites for establishing a security context. Callers refer to them indirectly through handles and never touch the credential elements. A caller may pass GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL to act as a default principal, and the RFC recommends an ordered set of default-resolution rules for portability.

Tokens are opaque data elements that the caller carries between peers: context-level tokens set up and manage a security context, and per-message tokens protect data on an established context. The caller transports tokens however it likes, in-band or out-of-band, and must tell token types apart.

A security context is established between peers. Several can coexist between the same pair, which allows graceful rollover when credentials expire. A mechanism type (mech_type) identifies the underlying technology and is represented as an Object Identifier. Callers are recommended to request the default mech_type.

Names are treated as opaque objects in internal, flat (tagged by OID) or Exported Name Object forms. Calls exist to compare, display, import, canonicalize, export and duplicate names. Optional channel bindings let a caller tie context establishment to properties of the underlying channel, such as addresses, to limit reuse of an intercepted establishment token.
sections.eli5: Credentials are your ID card. Tokens are sealed notes you pass to the other side. A context is the private conversation you set up once you trust each other.

sections.title: Establishing a Context and Protecting Messages
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, the client calls GSS_Init_sec_context() with the mutual authentication flag set and gets back an output_token and GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED. It sends the token to the server, which passes it to GSS_Accept_sec_context(). That call returns GSS_S_COMPLETE, the client's authenticated name, and a token for the client. The client feeds that token to a further GSS_Init_sec_context() call, which returns GSS_S_COMPLETE.

The client then calls GSS_Wrap() to apply data origin authentication, integrity and optionally confidentiality, and the server calls GSS_Unwrap() to reverse it. The server can finish with GSS_Delete_sec_context(), optionally producing a token that the client passes to GSS_Process_context_token().

Every call returns a mechanism-independent major_status (such as GSS_S_COMPLETE, GSS_S_FAILURE, GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED) and a mechanism-specific minor_status. Optional per-message replay detection and sequencing report GSS_S_DUPLICATE_TOKEN, GSS_S_OLD_TOKEN, GSS_S_UNSEQ_TOKEN and GSS_S_GAP_TOKEN; detecting these does not stop the message being delivered, so what to do is caller policy. The context flags integ_avail and conf_avail tell the caller which protection is available, and a FALSE integ_avail means wrapping applies no cryptographic protection.

Version 2 also adds anonymous initiators (anon_req_flag, which a mechanism need not honor) and prot_ready_state, which can allow per-message protection before establishment finishes. A quality-of-protection parameter lets mechanisms offer different protection levels, though non-default values are non-portable.
sections.eli5: You and a friend swap a few sealed notes to prove who you are. After that you can pass each other locked messages that only the two of you can open.

sections.title: The Four Groups of Calls
sections.content:
The interface is divided into four groups. Credential management calls acquire, release, inspect and incrementally build credentials (GSS_Acquire_cred, GSS_Release_cred, GSS_Inquire_cred, GSS_Add_cred, GSS_Inquire_cred_by_mech).

Context-level calls initiate, accept and delete contexts, process control tokens, report remaining lifetime, inquire about a context, find the wrap size limit, and export or import a context between processes. Per-message calls are GSS_GetMIC and GSS_VerifyMIC (an integrity check carried as a separate token) and GSS_Wrap and GSS_Unwrap (sign, optionally encrypt and encapsulate the message). Support calls handle names, status display, mechanism lists and OID sets.

The RFC notes that per-message primitives work on protocol data units and are not an efficient fit for stream protocols such as Telnet if cryptography must be applied octet by octet. It also defines no initialization calls, so implementations must be self-initializing.
sections.eli5: The tools come in four drawers: ID cards, starting a conversation, locking each message, and handy helpers.

sections.title: Token Format and Name Types
sections.content:
The first token of a context establishment sequence must begin with a mechanism-independent tag for standards-track mechanisms. The tag is the byte 0x60, a length, the byte 0x06 (object identifier), the OID length and the OID octets, immediately followed by the mechanism-defined token. This is derived from ASN.1 and DER but is described directly in octets so implementers need no general ASN.1 code.

Exported names use the OID {1 3 6 1 5 6 4} and a layout with a 2-byte token identifier (hex 04 01), a 2-byte mechanism OID length, the OID, a 4-byte name length, and the name.

Section 4 defines mechanism-independent name types: the host-based service form service@hostname (GSS_C_NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE, where the hostname is canonicalized by DNS and lower-cased), the user name form, the machine UID form and the string UID form. Section 5 sketches how the API could be realized over Kerberos V5 (single and double TGT) and X.509 mechanisms, as illustration only.
sections.eli5: Every first note starts with a small label saying which kind of lock is in use, so the other side knows how to open it.

sections.title: Compatibility with Version 1
sections.content:
The memo intends that GSS-V1 (RFC 1508) callers can work atop GSS-V2 providers, and all V1 calls are preserved. The V1 per-message names are deprecated: GSS_Seal, GSS_Sign, GSS_Unseal and GSS_Verify give way to GSS_Wrap, GSS_GetMIC, GSS_Unwrap and GSS_VerifyMIC.

New in V2 are credential calls (GSS_Add_cred, GSS_Inquire_cred_by_mech), context calls (GSS_Inquire_context, GSS_Wrap_size_limit, GSS_Export_sec_context, GSS_Import_sec_context), many name and OID support calls, three context state values (anon_state, prot_ready_state, trans_state) and extra status codes. Appendix A strongly recommends that mechanisms offering per-message protection also offer replay detection or sequencing. The security considerations section says only that security issues are discussed throughout the memo.
sections.eli5: The new version still works with programs written for the old one, and adds a few extra tools.
